title: Linear Momentum and Collisions
learning_objectives: Define linear momentum and give it a direction.
Relate impulse to the change in momentum.
Apply conservation of momentum to collisions, and tell elastic from inelastic.

sections.title: Introduction to Linear Momentum and Collisions
objectives: Describe what momentum adds to the description of a collision.

misconceptions.claim: Momentum is just another word for speed.
misconceptions.correction: Momentum is mass times velocity, so a heavy body moving slowly can carry as much momentum as a light one moving fast.

summary: Momentum measures how hard it is to stop a body.
Collisions are where momentum conservation does its work.
Momentum is a vector, so direction matters.
sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source carries no worked example for this section and no solved exercise to promote, so the practice is left to the exercises themselves.

sections.title: Linear Momentum and Force
objectives: Compute the linear momentum of a body and give it a direction.

misconceptions.claim: The momentum of a body depends only on its speed.
misconceptions.correction: It depends on the mass as well: p = mv, so doubling the mass doubles the momentum.

summary: p = mv, and it is a vector.
Momentum is measured in kilogram metres per second.
The momentum of a system of particles is the vector sum of the momenta.

sections.title: Impulse
objectives: Relate impulse to the change in momentum, and compute both for a collision.

misconceptions.correction: Impulse is the force applied over the time it acts, so it is the change in momentum.

summary: J = F dt, and the impulse equals the change in momentum.
A longer contact time means a smaller force for the same change.
This is why a cricket bat hurts more than a ball.

sections.title: Conservation of Momentum
objectives: Apply conservation of momentum to a collision in which no external force acts.

misconceptions.claim: Momentum is conserved in every collision.
misconceptions.correction: It is conserved when the net external force on the system is zero, which is nearly true for a short collision.

summary: The total momentum before the collision equals the total momentum after it.
Momentum is conserved in all directions at once, unlike kinetic energy.
It holds for the system, not for each body.

sections.title: Elastic Collisions in One Dimension
objectives: Solve a one dimensional elastic collision and show that kinetic energy is conserved as well.

misconceptions.claim: In an elastic collision the bodies bounce apart with no change in speed.
misconceptions.correction: They exchange speed, so the speeds of the two bodies change while the total kinetic energy stays the same.

summary: An elastic collision conserves both momentum and kinetic energy.
The two bodies exchange velocities in the one dimensional case.
The relative speed of approach equals the relative speed of separation.

sections.title: Inelastic Collisions in One Dimension
objectives: Solve a one dimensional inelastic collision, where the bodies stick together or lose energy.

misconceptions.claim: In an inelastic collision the momentum is not conserved.
misconceptions.correction: Momentum is still conserved. What is lost is kinetic energy, and it goes into heat, sound and deformation.

summary: Momentum is conserved in an inelastic collision too.
Kinetic energy is not, and the difference becomes internal energy.
A completely inelastic collision leaves the bodies moving together.

sections.title: Collisions of Point Masses in Two Dimensions
objectives: Solve a two dimensional collision using the components of momentum.

misconceptions.claim: Momentum is only conserved in a straight line collision.
misconceptions.correction: Momentum is conserved in every direction. In two dimensions the components are conserved separately.

summary: The x and the y components of momentum are conserved separately.
The kinetic energy tells you whether the collision is elastic.
The geometry of the components is what the two dimensional problems are really about.

definition.text: The product of the mass of a body and its velocity, a vector measured in kilogram metres per second.
The product of a force and the time it acts, equal to the change in momentum it produces.
A collision in which both the total momentum and the total kinetic energy are conserved.
A collision in which the total momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not.

exam_traps.correction: Momentum is the product of the mass and the velocity, and it is a vector.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: Impulse is the force divided by the time it acts.
exam_traps.correction: Impulse is the force multiplied by the time, and it equals the change in momentum.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: Momentum is conserved only in a collision where the bodies bounce apart.
exam_traps.correction: Momentum is conserved in every collision where the net external force is negligible, whether or not the bodies bounce.

exam_traps.subject: physics
exam_traps.misconception: In an elastic collision only the momentum is conserved.
exam_traps.correction: In an elastic collision the total kinetic energy is conserved as well, and the bodies exchange speed.
exam_traps.signal: Our own question offers the conservation of the momentum alone as an option.

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A body of mass 4 kg moves at 3 m/s. What is its momentum?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Momentum is mass times velocity, so p = 4 x 3 = 12 kg m/s.
exam_recall_checks.source: authored against the JAMB physics syllabus

exam_recall_checks.subject: physics
exam_recall_checks.stem: A force of 20 N acts on a body for 5 s. What is the impulse?
exam_recall_checks.explanation: Impulse is force times time, so J = 20 x 5 = 100 N s, and that is the change in momentum.
